newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FOCUS-Taiwan aims silicon sling at DRAM king Korea.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Taiwan aims silicon sling at DRAM king Korea.

text.p: Taiwan's microchip makers admit they must still rely on foreign know-how to stay in the game as the development of next-generation memory chips shakes up the competitive global market.

But describing themselves as resourceful Davids to South Korea's ungainly Goliath, the island's firms hope to eventually usurp the South Koreans as the trendsetters of the global semiconductor industry.

For now, they aim to compensate for a lack of expertise with superior efficiency as the global industry, led by South Korea's Samsung Electronics Co, upgrades production to advanced 64-megabit dynamic random access memory chips from 16-megabit DRAMs.
"For the next few years I think most Taiwan firms will have to rely on foreign companies to make 64-megabit DRAMs," said Winbond Electronics vice-president Archie Yeh.

"What we can do to compete is, once we get the technological capability, make the chips faster and more efficiently," Yeh told Reuters in an interview at Winbond headquarters in northern Taiwan's high-tech Hsinchu science park.
Winbond, which receives technological assistance from Japan's Toshiba Corp, plans to begin producing 64-megabit DRAMs in 1998.
Winbond is one of a host of Taiwan chipmakers that will rely on Japanese assistance to launch 64-megabit DRAMs in 1998.
"Developing DRAMs by yourself is hard because it demands a lot of investment," said Yeh.

Another 64-megabit hopeful is neophyte Powerchip Co, a joint venture of Japan's Mitsubishi Electric and Taiwan's Umax-Elite Group. Powerchip vice-president Ben Tseng agreed that Taiwan must still follow the lead of Japan and South Korea.

But he predicted it would be only a matter of time before Taiwan struck out on its own, noting that it had supplanted South Korea as world leader in computer monitor production as well as motherboards.
"Taiwan has always been very strong in manufacturing commodities and DRAMs will in effect become commodities," Tseng said.

"It's a David versus Goliath competition. South Korea's giant chipmakers like Samsung have all the muscle, but they do not have the flexibility to match Taiwan companies for manufacturing efficiency," he added.

Exemplifying this emphasis on efficiency, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co has become the island's top chipmaker by running its operations entirely on foundry services that cater to the specifications of each customer.

Taiwan Semiconductor's affiliate Vanguard International Semiconductor will not abandon the competitive DRAM market, and plans to churn out 64-megabit DRAMs along with the rest of the prominent chipmakers come 1998.

According to Taiwan's Institute for Information Industry, Taiwan produced 9.9 percent of the world's DRAMs in 1996 -- making it the world's fourth-largest supplier behind the United States, which made 10.9 percent.
South Korea ranked first with a 43.5 percent market share, followed by Japan at 30.3 percent.
